question: I got called for jury duty next month. Do I have to use my annual leave for it?
answer: You are entitled to paid time off without charge to leave for jury service, as stated in 5 U.S.C. 6322. However, if your jury duty is considered an exigency of the public business, you may forfeit annual leave. If this occurs, you must schedule and use the restored annual leave no later than the end of the leave year ending two years after the termination date of the exigency. You are not automatically exempt from using annual leave for jury duty, but you are entitled to paid time off without losing your leave entitlement.
gold_answer: No. Federal employees summoned as jurors get court leave with no loss of pay or leave [5 U.S.C. 6322(a)].

question: I'm in the Army Reserve. How many days of paid military leave do I get each year, and can I carry over what I don't use?
answer: The provided policy documents do not cover this. I can help with US federal leave, pay, holiday and related HR rules.
gold_answer: Reservists get 20 days of paid military leave per fiscal year (160 hours for a full-time employee), and up to 20 unused days carry over to the next fiscal year [5 U.S.C. 6323(a)(1)].

question: My brother was killed while serving in a combat zone. How much paid time off can I get to attend his funeral?
answer: You are entitled to up to 3 workdays of funeral leave to make arrangements for or to attend the funeral of your brother, who died as a result of wounds, disease, or injury incurred while serving in a combat zone. This leave is granted without loss of pay or reduction in leave entitlements, and the 3 days need not be consecutive if you provide satisfactory reasons for nonconsecutive days [OPM fact sheet: Leave for Funerals and Bereavement > Funeral Leave for Combat-Related Death of an Immediate Relative].
gold_answer: Up to 3 workdays of funeral leave with no loss of pay or leave, for the funeral or memorial service of an immediate relative (brothers included) who died as a result of combat-zone service [5 U.S.C. 6326(a); 5 CFR 630.803].

question: I'm coming back to my federal job after a 3-month deployment supporting an overseas contingency operation. Do I get any paid time off to readjust?
answer: You are entitled to 5 days of excused absence upon your return from active duty in support of the Overseas Contingency Operations (OCO), such as a 3-month deployment. This excused absence is intended to aid in your readjustment to civilian life. The 5 days of excused absence must be granted immediately prior to your actual resumption of duties, not necessarily immediately before your return. [OPM fact sheet: 5 Days of Excused Absence for Employees Returning from Active Military Duty > Questions and Answers on Excused Absence for Employees Returning from Active Duty in the Overseas Contingency Operations]
gold_answer: Yes. Employees returning from at least 42 consecutive days of active duty in support of the Overseas Contingency Operations get 5 days of excused absence (paid) [OPM fact sheet: 5 Days of Excused Absence for Employees Returning from Active Military Duty].

question: I earned compensatory time off for travel on a work trip. How long do I have to use it before I lose it?
answer: The general rule is that an employee must use accrued compensatory time off for travel by the end of the 26th pay period after the pay period during which it was earned, or the employee must forfeit such compensatory time off, except in certain circumstances [OPM fact sheet: Compensatory Time Off > FLSA-nonexempt employees]. If the employee is unable to use the compensatory time off due to specific exceptions, such as uniformed service or an on-the-job injury, they may retain it [OPM fact sheet: Compensatory Time Off for Travel - Questions & Answers to Fact Sheet].
gold_answer: You must use it by the end of the 26th pay period after the pay period in which it was earned, or it is forfeited (an agency may extend this for an exigency) [5 CFR 550.1407(a)].

question: If I have to work on a federal holiday, how am I paid for those hours?
answer: If you are required to work on a federal holiday, you are entitled to holiday premium pay. Specifically, you are entitled to a minimum of 2 hours of holiday premium pay for work performed during basic (non-overtime) holiday hours. This is outlined in 5 U.S.C. 5546(c) and 5 CFR 550.131(c). Additionally, if you work more than 8 hours on a holiday, you are entitled to overtime pay at the same rate as for overtime work on other days. For further details, refer to the OPM fact sheet on Holidays, Work Schedules, and Pay.
gold_answer: You get your basic pay plus holiday premium pay equal to your rate of basic pay (double pay) for up to 8 hours of non-overtime holiday work [5 CFR 550.131(a)].

question: My job requires me to wear a uniform. What's the most my agency can give me each year as a uniform allowance?
answer: The maximum annual uniform allowance an agency can provide to an employee is $1,500 per year, as specified in 5 U.S.C. 5901. This allowance is intended to help defray the costs of purchasing uniforms required for official duties. Agencies are not obligated to provide the full $1,500 for every employee; instead, they should determine rates based on actual uniform needs and estimated costs for each category of employees, as outlined in 5 CFR part 591, subpart A.
gold_answer: Up to $1,500 a year, either as an allowance or as uniforms furnished at that cost (agencies may set lower rates based on actual need) [OPM fact sheet: Uniform Allowances Fact Sheet; 5 U.S.C. 5901].

question: I got a quality step increase last spring. How soon can I get another one?
answer:
To be eligible for another quality step increase (QSI), you must not have received a QSI within the preceding 52 consecutive calendar weeks [5 CFR 531.505]. This restriction applies to receiving a QSI, not to getting another one. The 52-week period is a limitation on the frequency of QSI awards, not a waiting period for eligibility. 

To be eligible for a QSI, you must also be below step 10 of your grade level and demonstrate sustained outstanding performance [OPM fact sheet: Quality Step Increase > Eligibility]. The timing of your next QSI will depend on meeting these criteria and the approval process.
gold_answer: Not within 52 consecutive calendar weeks of the last one [5 CFR 531.505].

question: When I retire, will I get paid for my unused sick leave the way I do for annual leave?
answer: When you retire, you will not receive payment for your unused sick leave in the same way as annual leave. According to OPM guidelines, a lump-sum payment for unused annual leave is provided upon retirement, but this does not include unused sick leave [OPM fact sheet: Fact Sheet: Lump-Sum Payments For Annual Leave > Fact Sheet: Lump-Sum Payments For Annual Leave]. Additionally, unused sick leave may be used in the calculation of your annuity if your separation is due to retirement or death in service [OPM fact sheet: Fact Sheet: Leave Upon Transfer or Separation > Fact Sheet: Leave Upon Transfer or Separation]. However, it is not included in any lump-sum payment.
gold_answer: No. Separating employees get a lump-sum payment for unused annual leave only; it does not include unused sick leave [OPM fact sheet: Lump-Sum Payments For Annual Leave].

question: A coworker has a medical emergency. What's the most annual leave I can donate through the voluntary leave transfer program this year?
answer: The most annual leave you can donate through the voluntary leave transfer program in a leave year is up to 104 hours. This limit applies to donations made to an emergency leave transfer program, and each agency may establish written criteria for waiving this limitation [5 CFR 630.1110(a) to 630.1110(b)]. Additionally, you may not donate more than one-half of the annual leave you would accrue during the leave year [OPM fact sheet: Voluntary Leave Transfer Program > Limitations on Leave Donations].
gold_answer: No more than one-half of the annual leave you would accrue during the leave year (less if you have use-or-lose leave) [5 CFR 630.908(a)].

question: If I'm laid off after 14 years of service, how is my severance pay worked out?
answer: The provided policy documents do not cover this. Your question about severance pay for being laid off after 14 years of service requires a human decision. A draft case has been created and is pending approval. You can expect further details once it is reviewed by an HR specialist.
gold_answer: One week of basic pay for each full year of service up to 10 years, plus two weeks for each full year beyond 10 (here 10 + 8 = 18 weeks before any age adjustment), with a lifetime cap of 52 weeks [5 CFR 550.707].

question: I've used up all my annual leave. Can my agency advance me more, and how much?
answer: An agency may advance annual leave to an employee at its discretion, but the amount cannot exceed what the employee would accrue within the leave year. The agency should not advance leave if it is known or reasonably expected that the employee will not return to duty, such as in cases of disability retirement. The agency must consider factors like the expectation of return to duty, the need for the employee's services, and the benefits to the agency of retaining the employee. The exact amount of leave that can be advanced depends on the employee's accrued leave and the agency's discretion. For specific calculations, you may need to consult your agency's HR department.
gold_answer: At its discretion, an agency may advance annual leave up to the amount you would accrue within the leave year [OPM fact sheet: Advanced Annual Leave].

question: I'm a disabled veteran and need unpaid time off for medical treatment. Can my supervisor turn down my LWOP request?
answer: As a disabled veteran, you are entitled to use sick leave, annual leave, or leave without pay (LWOP) for necessary medical treatment associated with your service-connected disability. There is no explicit entitlement to LWOP, but you may use LWOP if it is necessary for medical treatment. Your supervisor may deny your request if they believe it does not meet the criteria for medical treatment, but the specific criteria for medical treatment are not clearly defined in the evidence. If you believe your request was denied unfairly, you may need to escalate the matter to HR for further review.
gold_answer: No. Disabled veterans are entitled to leave without pay for necessary medical treatment (Executive Order 5396) [OPM fact sheet: Leave Without Pay].

question: My husband is in the Reserve and just got deployment orders with only 5 days' notice. Can I take FMLA leave to deal with it, and for how long?
answer: Your husband's short-notice deployment qualifies for FMLA leave under the "short-notice deployment" category, which is covered under 5 CFR 630.1204(a)(1)(i). According to the policy, you may take up to 7 calendar days of FMLA leave to address issues arising from the deployment, beginning on the date your husband is notified of the deployment. You should contact your employer's HR department to initiate the FMLA leave process and provide the necessary documentation.
gold_answer: Yes. Short-notice deployment (notice of 7 or fewer days) is a qualifying exigency; you can take up to 7 calendar days starting on the date he was notified [5 CFR 630.1204(a)(1)].

question: If I lose use-or-lose annual leave because of a work emergency, what must I have done to get it restored?
answer: If you lose use-or-lose annual leave due to a work emergency, it cannot be restored under the standard conditions. However, there are limited circumstances under which forfeited use-or-lose annual leave may be restored, such as if the employee was performing mission-critical work in response to a national emergency as determined by OPM, or if there was an administrative error or prolonged sickness of the employee [OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave > Importance of Scheduling "Use or Lose" Leave in Advance]. If you believe your situation falls under one of these exceptions, you should contact your agency's HR office to discuss your case further.
gold_answer: The leave must have been scheduled in writing before the start of the third biweekly pay period before the end of the leave year [5 CFR 630.308(a)].

question: We're adopting a child and I have a lot of sick leave saved. Is there a limit on how much of it I can use for the adoption?
answer: There is no limitation on the amount of sick leave that may be used for adoption-related purposes. Sick leave for adoption-related purposes does not count towards the 104-hour (13-day) limit of sick leave each leave year for family care and bereavement purposes or the overall limit of 12 weeks of sick leave each leave year for all family care purposes [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave for Adoption > Sick Leave Usage Limits per Leave Year]. You may use your saved sick leave for adoption-related purposes without any restrictions.
gold_answer: No. There is no limit on sick leave used for adoption-related purposes, and it does not count toward the 104-hour family care and bereavement limit [OPM fact sheet: Sick Leave for Adoption; 5 U.S.C. 6307(c)].

question: My position is being downgraded after a reclassification. How long do I keep my current grade?
answer: When an employee is placed in a lower-graded position due to a reclassification, they are entitled to retain the grade held immediately before the reduction for a period of 2 years, as stated in the OPM fact sheet on Grade Retention [OPM fact sheet: Grade Retention > Period of Grade Retention]. During this period, the employee is entitled to 50 percent of the increase in the maximum rate of the highest applicable rate range for the employee's position and retained grade.
gold_answer: You are entitled to retain your previous grade for 2 years [OPM fact sheet: Grade Retention].

question: I'm a criminal investigator. What rate is availability pay paid at?
answer: Availability pay is paid at 25 percent of a criminal investigator's rate of basic pay, as defined in 5 CFR 550.103. This rate applies to the unscheduled duty hours that the criminal investigator is required to work or be available to work. However, it is subject to the maximum earnings limitation on premium pay for law enforcement officers under 5 U.S.C. 5547(c). [5 CFR 550.185(a)]
gold_answer: Availability pay is fixed by law at 25 percent of the criminal investigator's rate of basic pay [OPM fact sheet: Availability Pay].

question: I'm full-time with 10 years of service. How many hours of annual leave will I earn over a full leave year?
answer: As a full-time employee with 10 years of service, you will earn **160 hours** of annual leave over a full leave year [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)]. Additionally, you may carry over up to **240 hours** of unused annual leave to the next leave year [5 U.S.C. 6304].
gold_answer: 160 hours: 6 hours in each of 25 pay periods plus 10 hours in the last pay period [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)(2)].

question: I'm in the Senior Executive Service. How much annual leave do I earn each pay period?
answer: As a member of the Senior Executive Service (SES), you accrue annual leave at the rate of 1 day (8 hours) for each full biweekly pay period, as stated in the OPM fact sheet [OPM fact sheet: Annual Leave Accrual Rates for Senior Executive Service, Senior Level and Scientific or Professional Positions, or Equivalent Pay Systems > Fact Sheet: Annual Leave Accrual Rates for Senior Executive Service, Senior Level and Scientific or Professional Positions, or Equivalent Pay Systems] [opm-fs-annual-leave-accrual-rates-for-senior-executive-service-senior-level-and-scientific-or-professional-positions-or-equivalent-pay-systems-fact-sheet-annual-leave-accrual-rates-for-senior-executive-s-1]. This rate applies without regard to your length of service with the Federal Government.
gold_answer: 8 hours (1 day) per biweekly pay period, regardless of years of service [5 U.S.C. 6303(f)].

question: I'm part-time with 1 year of service and had 60 hours in a pay status this pay period. How much annual and sick leave did I earn?
answer: Based on your part-time status and 1 year of service, you earned **3 hours of annual leave** and **3 hours of sick leave** this pay period. These accruals are calculated at a rate of 1 hour for every 20 hours in a pay status [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)] for annual leave and [5 U.S.C. 6307(a)] for sick leave. The maximum annual leave carryover is 240 hours [5 U.S.C. 6304].
gold_answer: 3 hours of annual leave (1 hour per 20 hours in pay status, under 3 years of service) and 3 hours of sick leave (1 hour per 20 hours) [5 U.S.C. 6303(a); 6307(a)].

question: I'm a federal employee stationed overseas and I'll have 420 hours of annual leave at the end of the leave year. How many hours will I lose?
answer: As a federal employee stationed overseas, you are allowed a maximum annual leave carryover of 360 hours [5 U.S.C. 6304]. Since you have 420 hours of annual leave at the end of the leave year, you will lose 60 hours of annual leave.
gold_answer: 60 hours: overseas employees can carry over up to 360 hours (45 days), so 420 - 360 = 60 [5 U.S.C. 6304(b)].

question: Which federal holidays fall in November 2028?
answer:
In November 2028, the federal holidays are:

gold_answer: 5 x $48.80 = $244.00 [OPM 2026 GS pay table (RUS)]

question: I'm a GS-12 step 5 in the Washington DC area and I'm scheduled to work 8 hours on Thanksgiving 2026. How much holiday premium pay will I get on top of my regular pay?
answer:
For each hour of holiday work, employees receive holiday premium pay in addition to their rate of basic pay. Holiday premium pay is equal to an employee's rate of basic pay. Therefore, if you are required to work on a holiday, you will receive double your rate of basic pay for each hour worked. 

Your rate of basic pay for a GS-12, step 5, in the Washington DC area is $55.62 per hour [OPM 2026 General Schedule pay table (DCB)]. Thus, your holiday premium pay will be $55.62 per hour. 

If you work 8 hours on Thanksgiving 2026, you will receive $55.62 * 8 = $444.96 in holiday premium pay in addition to your regular pay for that day.
gold_answer: Holiday premium pay equals your basic rate: 8 x $55.62 = $444.96 on top of your basic pay (total $889.92 for the day) [5 CFR 550.131(a); OPM 2026 GS pay table (DCB)].

question: I've been full-time for 7 years and I'll have 275 hours of annual leave at the end of the leave year. How many hours will I forfeit?
answer: You will forfeit 35 hours of annual leave. The maximum annual leave carryover allowed is 240 hours, and you currently have 275 hours. Therefore, you will forfeit 275 - 240 = 35 hours [5 U.S.C. 6304].
gold_answer: 35 hours: the carryover limit is 240 hours, so 275 - 240 = 35 [5 U.S.C. 6304(a)].

question: I have 10 years of full-time service and there are 6 pay periods left in the leave year, including the last one. How much more annual leave will I earn this year?
answer: With 10 years of full-time service, you will earn 6 hours of annual leave for each of the remaining 6 pay periods. This means you will earn a total of 36 hours of annual leave this year. [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)]
gold_answer: 40 hours: 6 hours in each of 5 pay periods plus 10 hours in the last pay period [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)(2)].

question: I've been full-time for 2 years. How much annual leave do I earn per pay period? ||| What about once I pass 3 years?
answer: After 3 years of full-time service, you earn 6 hours of annual leave per pay period [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)]. Additionally, in the last full biweekly pay period of the leave year, you may earn up to 10 hours [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)]. The annual leave carryover cap remains at 240 hours [5 U.S.C. 6304].
gold_answer: 6 hours per pay period (10 hours in the last pay period of the year) for 3 to 15 years of service [5 U.S.C. 6303(a)(2)].
